variables.name: ERPNEXT_SITE_NAME
variables.purpose: Name of the single ERPNext site, and the value the image's nginx pins `FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER` to (`server_name`, the `X-Frappe-Site-Name` upstream header and the `try_files /<site>/public/...` prefix all read it). The platform derives it from the instance's own route host — `<slug>.<SEAMNEX_INGRESS_DOMAIN>`, `erpnext.seamnex.localhost` here — and that slug is the one the entry's `integration.apiBaseUrl` names, so the site and the API address describe the same deployment. A mismatch does not break the deployment, it produces links that point at a host the browser cannot resolve. A **bare host, with no scheme and no port**: the value is a Frappe *site name*, so it names the directory `sites/<name>`, the argument to `bench new-site`, nginx's `server_name` and the `try_files /<name>/public/` prefix. `http://erpnext.seamnex.localhost:8443` is not a valid site name and fails the first boot at `bench new-site` instead of producing a site — the same URL-shaped mistake the D9 default carried, there rejected by Rails with `400 Invalid host_name configuration`. The absolute URLs the product prints come from `ERPNEXT_SITE_ORIGIN`, not from this value: this one names the site, that one names the origin.
variables.constraint: Valid hostname (letters, digits, dots, dashes); no scheme, no port; created once on first start and not renamed afterwards

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SITE_ORIGIN
variables.purpose: Origin the product builds every absolute URL from — it is written to `host_name` in the site's `site_config.json`, which Frappe reads for password-reset links, notification and email bodies, print/export downloads and the post-login redirect. The platform derives it from the instance's own route as `scheme://<host>[:port]`, and the definition re-applies it on **every** start, so a route change reaches a running site at its next restart; promoted here from the first-boot bootstrap, which set it once to `http://<ERPNEXT_SITE_NAME>` and then never again — on a TLS edge at `:8443` that value sent every printed link to a plain-HTTP port nothing listens on, and on any later host change to the previous host. It is deliberately not the same value as `ERPNEXT_SITE_NAME`: that one is a Frappe *site name* (a directory and a `server_name`, no scheme, no port), this one is a URL. Frappe appends the path itself, so a trailing slash or a path belongs to neither.
variables.constraint: Absolute URL, no trailing slash and no path; the port is present only when the edge publishes one

rule.patternDescription: an absolute URL with no trailing slash and no path

variables.name: ERPNEXT_DATABASE_HOST
variables.purpose: Host of the MariaDB server the site is created on. The vendored definition ships that server as the `erpnext-db` service, so the default is the service name; override it only to install against a database the platform does not manage.
variables.constraint: Hostname or IP address reachable from the backend container

variables.name: ERPNEXT_DATABASE_PORT
variables.purpose: Port of that server. 3306 is what `bench new-site` expects for a MariaDB service and what the vendored database container listens on.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_REDIS_CACHE
variables.purpose: Redis URL used for the cache and the realtime (socket.io) channel: the definition writes it to both `redis_cache` and `redis_socketio` in `common_site_config.json`, which is where Frappe's own fallback puts the socket.io pub/sub channel when the second key is absent. The two must not be separated onto different instances by accident — pointing socket.io at the queue instance means a queue purge silently drops every open realtime connection. The vendored definition ships a dedicated `erpnext-redis-cache` service; a shared Redis works but then a cache flush also drops queued background jobs.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_REDIS_QUEUE
variables.purpose: Redis URL used for the background job queue drained by the two workers. It is written into `common_site_config.json` on every start, so a change reaches a running instance without reinstalling the site.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_DATABASE_ROOT_PASSWORD
variables.purpose: Password of the MariaDB privileged account `bench new-site` uses to create the site database and its own account. The image's entrypoint has no fallback for it, so an unset value leaves the database container refusing to start and the site never created. It is also read on **every** start, not only the first: `bench new-site` binds the site's own account to the client address of the container that ran it (`DbManager.get_current_host`), so a recreated container — reconfigure, upgrade, route change — would answer `Access denied` for a site whose database is perfectly intact. The bootstrap therefore re-creates that account for the address the container has now. Stored in the platform secret store and injected at apply time; it never enters the render set.
variables.constraint: At least 16 characters; independent of the site's own database password, which `bench new-site` generates inside the product

variables.name: ERPNEXT_ADMIN_PASSWORD
variables.purpose: Password of the `Administrator` account the first-boot bootstrap creates. Read once, on the first install; later accounts and their roles are managed inside the product. Sign-in beyond that first account is meant to go through the platform identity provider (the entry's `native` guarantee class), and the platform's SSO registration is what makes that true — the account itself stays as the break-glass path, which is why it is still required.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_ENABLED
variables.purpose: Whether the first boot writes a `Social Login Key` and turns on Frappe's social sign-in (`enable_social_login`). Frappe reads identity settings from a site-database row, never from the environment, so this is the switch the bootstrap obeys rather than a value the product consumes itself. `false` leaves the site exactly as the installer made it: password sign-in only, which is the declared fallback and not a broken state.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_CLIENT_ID
variables.purpose: Client id the site presents to the identity provider — the `client_id` of the `Social Login Key`. The platform derives it as `seamnex-<instance slug>`, the same name `registerIdentity` registers in Keycloak, so the two halves cannot drift; the default names exactly one deployment and is only what the entry screen shows before an instance exists.
variables.constraint: `seamnex-<instance slug>`; must equal the client id the platform registered
variables.conditional: Required when ERPNEXT_SSO_ENABLED is true; derived from the route slug at deploy time.

rule.patternDescription: seamnex-<slug>, lower-case letters, digits and hyphens

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_CLIENT_SECRET
variables.purpose: Client secret shared with the identity provider; the bootstrap stores it in the site's `Social Login Key`, and Frappe refuses to show the sign-in button when the stored secret is empty (`www/login.py` skips a key whose password does not decrypt). Leave it empty and the platform mints one at deploy time and writes it back here, which is what keeps the product's secret and Keycloak's registration equal. Without a value and without a minted one the bootstrap writes nothing and password sign-in stays in place.
variables.constraint: 24–128 characters, at least one letter and one digit
variables.conditional: Required when ERPNEXT_SSO_ENABLED is true; generated by the platform when left empty.

rule.patternDescription: letters, digits and ._~- only, with at least one of each

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_BASE_URL
variables.purpose: Issuer of the realm, as the *instance network* reaches it (`http://keycloak:8080/realms/seamnex`). Two things read it: the sign-in page, which renders a provider button only when `base_url` is set, and the platform's own `sso_login` probe, which fetches `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration` from inside the instance network. It is deliberately not the browser's view of the IdP — the product talks to the issuer server-to-server, and the browser leg is `ERPNEXT_SSO_AUTHORIZE_URL`.
variables.constraint: Absolute URL of the realm, reachable from the instance network, no trailing slash

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_AUTHORIZE_URL
variables.purpose: Authorization endpoint the *browser* is sent to — the one leg of the flow that must be reachable from a workstation, not from the container. Frappe puts this value on the sign-in button's URL as-is (`Social Login Key.authorize_url`), so it has to carry the IdP's published origin. Splitting it from the token and userinfo endpoints is the same split EspoCRM's declaration makes.
variables.constraint: Absolute URL the browser can reach

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_TOKEN_URL
variables.purpose: Token endpoint the site calls server-to-server to exchange the authorization code. Internal origin, because the exchange never involves a browser; it must be the same realm as the authorize URL or Keycloak rejects the code with `invalid_grant`.
variables.constraint: Absolute URL of the same realm as ERPNEXT_SSO_AUTHORIZE_URL

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_USERINFO_URL
variables.purpose: Userinfo endpoint the site reads after the token exchange. This response, not the ID token, supplies the attributes Frappe maps onto a user: `email` (falling back to `upn` then `unique_name`), `given_name`/`family_name`, and the id named by `ERPNEXT_SSO_USER_ID_PROPERTY`. Frappe does not verify an ID-token signature on this path, so the userinfo call is the whole trust anchor.
variables.constraint: Absolute URL of the same realm; must answer `email` for every user who may sign in

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_SCOPE
variables.purpose: Scope sent on the authorization request, space-separated, written into the `Social Login Key`'s `auth_url_data`. `openid` is what makes the provider issue an ID token and what makes `sub` stable for the account mapping; drop it and Keycloak answers the token request but the authorise leg loses OIDC semantics. `profile` and `email` carry the attributes the userinfo mapping reads.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_USER_ID_PROPERTY
variables.purpose: Claim the site stores as the provider's subject for a user (`Social Login Key.user_id_property`). Frappe falls back to `sub` when this is empty; overriding it to something mutable — an email, a username — means a rename inside the IdP creates a second account instead of finding the first. The mapping is written once per user and never reconciled, which is why `sub` is the default.
variables.constraint: A claim present in the userinfo response; `sub` unless the provider's subject is unstable

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_SIGN_UPS
variables.purpose: Whether a person who authenticates at the IdP but has no account on this site is created one (`Social Login Key.sign_ups`). `Allow` mirrors EspoCRM's `OIDC_CREATE_USER`: the first successful sign-in provisions the user from the userinfo response. `Deny` answers a 403 page — *Sorry. Signup from Website is disabled* — which is the setting for a site whose accounts are seeded deliberately. Either way an existing disabled user is refused, never re-enabled.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_DEFAULT_ROLE
variables.purpose: Role granted to a user the sign-in flow creates, written to `Portal Settings.default_role`. This is the only role a social login can confer, and Frappe applies it on *creation* only — an existing user's roles are never touched, so a mapping changed after someone's first sign-in reaches nothing. Frappe needs the role to exist already; an unknown role fails the login instead of being ignored. Empty leaves the site's own default, which is what an installation that manages roles by hand wants.
variables.constraint: Name of a Role that already exists on the site; empty leaves it unset

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SSO_DISABLE_LOCAL_LOGIN
variables.purpose: Whether the sign-in page stops offering a password form (`System Settings.disable_user_pass_login`), which is the fallback decision EspoCRM expresses as `OIDC_FALLBACK`. `false` — the default — keeps the local form beside the provider button, so an IdP outage does not lock an administrator out of the site they are meant to repair. `true` is the right setting only once the provider path has been proven on the instance, and it does not remove the `bench` break-glass either way.

variables.name: ERPNEXT_SESSION_EXPIRY
variables.purpose: Session lifetime as `HH:MM:SS`, written to `System Settings.session_expiry` — Frappe's only session-length setting, and the number the platform's residual-session statement (`integration.sessionMaxMinutes`, 480) claims to know. Frappe measures it as idle time and expires a session after it, so declaring it here is what makes the 480-minute claim true rather than assumed. The product default is 240 hours (`240:00:00`), four weeks of idle time on an ERP; eight hours is the working day the entry declares.
variables.constraint: HH:MM:SS, hours:minutes:seconds; must agree with integration.sessionMaxMinutes
